clinicalPearls: One of the more common glycolytic enzyme defects causing chronic non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia, second in frequency only to pyruvate kinase deficiency among glycolytic disorders
Inherited as an autosomal recessive trait, so a history of parental consanguinity or affected siblings is often present
Anaemia is Coombs-negative and typically presents from the neonatal period with jaundice, sometimes severe enough to require exchange transfusion
The blood film shows non-specific changes without the spherocytes of membrane disorders, reflecting a metabolic rather than structural defect
Some patients develop a neuromuscular phenotype with hypotonia and impaired motor development because the enzyme is expressed in tissues beyond the red cell
Diagnosis rests on demonstrating reduced enzyme activity on a red-cell enzyme assay and confirming a GPI mutation
Management is supportive with transfusion, folate supplementation and consideration of splenectomy in transfusion-dependent disease
reference.pathophysiology: Glucose phosphate isomerase catalyses the reversible interconversion of glucose-6-phosphate and fructose-6-phosphate, an early step of the glycolytic pathway that generates the ATP the mature red cell depends on entirely because it lacks mitochondria. When enzyme activity is deficient, glycolytic flux and ATP production fall, the red cell cannot sustain its ion pumps and membrane integrity, and it undergoes premature destruction, producing a chronic non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia. Because the enzyme is a housekeeping protein present in all tissues, severe deficiency can additionally impair neuromuscular function.
additionalDifferentials: Hereditary spherocytosis and other membrane disorders
Other glycolytic enzymopathies such as hexokinase deficiency
additionalInvestigations: Red-cell glucose phosphate isomerase enzyme activity assay
Full blood count with reticulocyte count and blood film examination
Haemolysis screen including bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase and haptoglobin
Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test to exclude immune haemolysis
Molecular genetic testing of the GPI gene
Family studies including parental enzyme levels
redFlags: Severe neonatal jaundice risking kernicterus and requiring urgent exchange transfusion
Aplastic crisis precipitated by parvovirus B19 infection
Progressive neuromuscular impairment in severe deficiency
reference.prognosis: Prognosis varies with residual enzyme activity; many patients have a moderate, well-compensated anaemia with a normal lifespan, while those with severe deficiency and neuromuscular involvement have a more guarded outlook and greater transfusion dependence.
pitfalls: Assuming a structural membrane disorder when spherocytes are absent, rather than pursuing enzyme assays
Overlooking associated neuromuscular signs that point to a systemic enzymopathy
Failing to monitor for and treat transfusional iron overload
Attributing neonatal jaundice solely to blood-group incompatibility without a haemolysis workup
management: Provide supportive management of the chronic non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia with red-cell transfusion for symptomatic or poorly compensated anaemia
Give regular folic acid supplementation to support the increased erythropoietic turnover
Treat severe neonatal jaundice with phototherapy and, when needed, exchange transfusion to prevent kernicterus
In transfusion-dependent disease monitor for iron overload and institute iron chelation, and consider splenectomy in selected severe cases with prior vaccination and subsequent antibiotic prophylaxis
Monitor the full blood count, reticulocytes and haemolytic markers, and where a neuromuscular phenotype is present assess motor development and neurological function
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance, including parental carrier testing and family studies
